source.title: From Insight to Intervention: Interpretable Neuron Steering for Controlling Popularity Bias in Recommender Systems

record.tranche_reason: The study uses prior claims about SAE neuron specialization as motivation for a recommender-system method, then reports how its own neuron steering performs. It does not test the listed audit, language-model, vision-model, attribution-graph, or explanation-scoring claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports analyses of popularity-aligned SAE neurons and interventions on them in recommender systems. It does not independently test whether most neuron poles have one nameable job, nor does it evaluate the listed versions. General method-comparison results, including Figure 2 and Table 5, are not recorded as claim-version findings; Table 5 compares the paper's proposed method with its ablations. SAE reconstruction results in Table 3 do not test V5's attribution-graph claim.
record.test_reason: The study trains a TopK SAE on a SASRec recommender's user embeddings, picks popularity-responsive SAE latents with Cohen's d, and steers them to improve exposure fairness. It assumes SAE monosemanticity from cited work and reports its own method's performance. It does not audit what share of a model's own neurons have one job (V1, V2). It does not touch vision neurons (V3, V4), attribution graphs (V5), or explanation prediction and simulation scoring (V6, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAE-based steering of popularity-linked latents improves exposure fairness with minimal accuracy loss and offers interpretable, fine-grained control. The Yelp caveat is that IPR and DUOR reach larger fairness gains, at a larger nDCG cost.
record.recipe_differences: This is a post-hoc recommender-system method: it trains an SAE to reproduce a recommender's user embeddings, identifies popularity-responsive SAE neurons using synthetic head/tail user profiles, and steers their activations. It is not a replication of the listed audits or explanation evaluations.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering strength and neuron-selection threshold are varied; the paper reports that stronger suppression of popularity-aligned neurons can reduce nDCG earlier and more sharply than amplification of unpopularity-aligned neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In the SAE on SASRec embeddings, the latents with the most extreme Cohen's d concentrate their top activations on real users with head-heavy or tail-heavy histories, on all three datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some SAE latents trained on recommender embeddings track users' popularity orientation.

fits_no_version.finding: Lowering popularity-aligned latents improves Gini, while lowering unpopularity-aligned latents worsens it, on all three datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering popularity-aligned SAE latents causally shifts recommender exposure fairness.

fits_no_version.finding: After steering, user embeddings move away from synthetic popular profiles and toward unpopular ones. The shift is large on ML-1M and BeerAdvocate and small on Yelp; the paper reports p<0.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent steering shifts recommender user embeddings toward tail-oriented profiles.

record.problems: The interpretation analysis selects only the most positive and most negative Cohen's d neurons and uses intentionally extreme synthetic user profiles. The paper's main experiments use recommender systems rather than language or vision models. The text reports significance as p < 0.01 for embedding-distribution changes but does not provide error bars for the figure-only neuron analyses.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2's overall method-comparison plots and Table 5's PopSteer-versus-ablation fairness metrics are not cataloged as independent tests of the listed claim versions; they report performance of the proposed recommender method and its variants. Table 3 reports SAE reconstruction quality, not an attribution-graph test.

untested.parts: The Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its shares of one-job, two-job and not-understood poles.
Neuron shares across dense and mixture-of-experts language models and across scale.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, the pose reading, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Effects of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons without a replacement model.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict held-out firing.
Scoring explanations by simulating activations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The 'neurons' studied are SAE latents fitted to a recommender, not the model's own neurons. Monosemanticity is assumed from cited work, not measured. Table 1's normality percentages concern activation distributions, not interpretability shares, so they do not bear on V1 or V2.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit, the shares of single-job, related-job, and not-understood neuron poles, and held-out explanation tests.
Language-model comparisons across architectures and scales, including dense and mixture-of-experts models.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose explanations, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and interpretability estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples predict held-out activation locations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by activation simulation on new text.
